pages.independentObservation: Lecture 30 title, Reinforcement Learning. Printed footer1; no technical assessment content.
Objectives: RL foundations and agent/environment/state/action/reward loop; policies and value functions; model-free Q-learning and practical application. Repeated by substantive slides.
Contents roadmap includes exploration/exploitation, model-based/model-free, Q-learning, example and Gymnasium. Not a separate technical premise.

Supervised labeled X,y maps X to y; unsupervised X seeks patterns. RL interaction provides evaluative rather than prescribed action labels. Learning with critic is conceptual feedback distinction, not necessarily actor-critic architecture.

Teacher table gives prescribed output/information in advance; critic evaluates chosen behavior and motivates learned intermediate-state values. Printed scarce/delayed feedback is typical, not universal requirement that rewards appear only at episode end.

Trial-and-error evaluates actions after execution; dog treat analogy. Diagram sends a_t from agent to environment and returns observation/state s_(t+1) and reward r_(t+1). Distinguish reward from correct-action prescription.
Agent is decision-maker, environment external interaction world. Robot/maze is example. Agent boundary is a modeling choice, not every robot component universally outside environment.

Action a_t belongs to action space A; maze choices up/down/left/right. Discrete button versus continuous steering angle. Continuous action space does not fit a finite action-column table without adaptation.

Observation feedback returns next state and numerical reward. State called complete environment description, but later observation o_t may be partial; do not identify arbitrary observation with complete Markov state.

Loop explicitly distinguishes observation o_t from state s_t; action leads next-state/observation and reward r_(t+1). An episode spans start to terminal in this episodic setting; termination and imposed truncation later need distinction.

Deterministic policy pi:S->A versus stochastic pi(a|s). SARSA on-policy evaluates behavior policy; Q-learning off-policy targets greedy next actions. Printed regardless of exploration must not imply convergence without adequate visits/learning-rate conditions.

Finite horizon source sum of T undiscounted rewards; infinite discounted return starts r_(t+1) coefficient1, then gamma,gamma². 0<=gamma<1; gamma0 immediate only; approaching1 longer horizon. Bounded rewards needed for generic finite infinite sum; finite horizon can also be discounted by choice.

Optimal value maximizes expected cumulative reward, not every realized episode. V*(s)=max_a Q*(s,a); Q* fixes first action then follows optimal continuation. Multiple maximizing actions/policies possible.

Bellman decomposition separates immediate reward from gamma times expected next optimal value using transition probabilities P(s_next|s,a). Current-action max uses optimal continuation implicitly; expectation must condition on current state/action. Greedy extraction from Q* differs from maximizing just immediate reward.

State-value Bellman max is over present action; action-value form fixes current action then maximizes next action. Probability-weighted next-state sum is not max over possible next states. pi* chooses argmax action, not the scalar maximum value; ties can permit more than one action.

Explore to gather information, exploit current value estimates. Printed highest immediate reward conflicts with long-term Q definition: exploitation of Q estimates cumulative return, not necessarily immediate reward. Excess exploitation misses alternatives, excessive random exploration can reduce achieved return; neither guarantees failure in all tasks.

Model-free TD learns from experienced transitions without supplied exact reward/transition model; model-based known-model planning examples value and policy iteration. Source complete knowledge/no exploration is an idealized case, not every learned-model method.

Q update is Q_old+eta[r_next+gamma max Q(next,action)-Q_old]. Target contains sampled immediate reward plus estimated continuation, not fully observed future. Learning-rate decay mentioned; convergence is conditional on tabular assumptions, coverage and suitable step sizes, not every finite run.

Pseudocode initializes Q once, resets state per episode, chooses epsilon-greedy action, steps environment, updates current Q(s,a), then advances state until terminal. Terminal continuation should be zero. epsilon exploration probability versus greedy branch1-epsilon; random exploration may also select greedy action.

3D reach example locates gripper and supplies target to Q-learning block, reaches target then separately closes gripper. Reaching reward alone does not prove learned grasping/contact mechanics or physical robot safety.

Gymnasium provides standardized reinforcement-learning environment interfaces, not a learning agent or a physics engine by itself. Its make, reset, step and render functions have distinct roles. Common interfaces help comparisons but do not themselves make experiments fair.

Gymnasium with MuJoCo provides virtual dynamics/contact/gravity environments before hardware deployment; simulation can reduce cost and risk without guaranteeing transfer or hardware safety. Multiple illustrated tasks are examples, not one environment.

The notebook installs gymnasium-robotics, mujoco and matplotlib using notebook !pip syntax. FetchReachDense-v4 has a 7-DOF arm and a four-component native action [dx,dy,dz,gripper], each normalized to [-1,1]. Dense reward is negative Euclidean distance, therefore non-positive and zero at exact coincidence, not strictly always negative. The source loosely calls Gymnasium the physics simulator; MuJoCo is the physics engine.

Imports gymnasium, gymnasium_robotics, numpy and matplotlib; register_envs followed by make FetchReachDense-v4. The statement that register_envs loads all physics models needs API qualification. Distance rewards arrive on environment steps, not necessarily rendered video frames.

NX=NY=NZ=8, BIN_SIZE=0.04, N_ACTIONS=6. The float32 action map is positive and negative x, y, z unit commands, each with fourth component zero. These are six discrete choices mapped to four-component normalized native commands, not six native action coordinates or one-metre moves. The 512 spatial bins are a compressed observation representation, not automatically a fully observed Markov state.

Q has shape (8,8,8,6), 3072 scalar entries, initialized once to zero; alpha=0.1, gamma=0.95, epsilon=0.5. State is tuple(clip(((desired_goal-achieved_goal+0.16)/0.04).astype(int),0,7)); int conversion truncates toward zero before clipping. At zero error bin index is 4, not a separate terminal state. Rewards list starts empty; 5000 episodes reset observations and per-episode total, not Q.

Inner loop range(50) is an upper bound when later break is considered, not an unconditional exactly-50 guarantee. Uniform random action 0..5 is selected when random draw < epsilon; otherwise first argmax Q[s]. Random branch can select the greedy action. env.step returns observation, reward, terminated, truncated, info. Source incorrectly equates terminated with touching goal and time limit with physics engine; verify actual FetchReach API semantics.

Update computes new compressed state, then Q[s][a] += alpha*(r+gamma*max(Q[s_next])-Q[s][a]), before s,total advance and break on terminated or truncated. The printed code bootstraps unconditionally; a true terminal target should omit continuation, whereas ordinary time-limit truncation is not identical to true termination. At s_next=s, the right side still uses pre-update values.

After each episode append total; epsilon=max(0.05,epsilon*0.998). Every 500 completed episodes print mean of last 100 episode totals and post-decay epsilon, not a 500-episode average. Displayed means are -7.06,-6.86,-7.41,-6.77,-6.14,-5.98,-5.24,-4.90,-3.87,-3.37, showing nonmonotonic learning. Decay floor persists; it never becomes purely greedy.

Smoothing uses np.convolve(rewards,np.ones(50)/50,mode=valid), producing 4951 values from 5000 totals. Default plotted indices start at zero and represent overlapping windows, not original episode labels. Curve generally rises from approximately -9 to -3/-4 but is not monotonic and does not reach zero. Improving finite-run reward does not prove an optimal policy, convergence or hardware safety, contrary to the strong prose claim.

Suggested improvements: 12 bins per axis with smaller bin size, more than 20000 episodes, deep RL, and a fourth gripper action. Code consistency requires changing hard-coded clipping bound 7 when using 12 bins and choosing offset/range coherently; 12^3*6=10368 entries, 3.375 times original. Deep approximation avoids this explicit table but does not eliminate dimensionality or guarantee success. FetchReach blocked-gripper semantics must be checked before claiming a fourth command activates grasping; grasping also needs a suitable task/reward.

Summary repeats RL interaction and evaluative reward, optimal action attaining maximal Q*, and model-free off-policy Q-learning. These are earlier concepts, not new independent coverage; optimality remains conditional, not established by the sample curve.
References only: Introduction to Machine Learning, Ethem Alpaydin; no additional examinable proposition.
Thank-you-only terminal slide, no examinable content.

conceptGroups.scope: Learning paradigms, evaluative versus prescriptive feedback, and dense versus delayed reward
Agent/environment boundary, action and observation directions, state versus observation, reward indexing, and episodes
Deterministic/stochastic policies, on/off-policy distinction, and visitation limitations
Finite return, discounted powers, gamma boundary, and a convergent continuing sum
Expected optimality, Q* versus V*, Bellman decomposition, transition conditioning, state-conditioned maxima, and ties
Exploration versus cumulative-value exploitation and the purpose of information gathering
Known-model planning versus sampled TD, Q target/error/update, convergence qualifications, initialization and epsilon-greedy probabilities
Reach/grasp stages, simulator/API/agent roles and limits of simulation claims
Seven arm DOFs versus action coordinates, distance reward sign/geometry, notebook setup and environment construction
Discrete/native action mapping, command-versus-bin scaling, table cardinality/storage, relative error encoding, clipping/aliasing and per-episode reset
Epsilon branch, argmax ties/negative values, step API, termination versus truncation, write-before-advance and TD arithmetic
Undiscounted logging, epsilon floor and logarithmic crossing, checkpoint/window interpretation and seed dependence
Valid rolling average length/alignment and finite noisy training-curve limitations
Grid cardinality/refinement consistency, deep approximation and blocked-gripper/task limitations
Integrated trace, continued non-greedy probability, estimated versus true optimal Q and optimistic initialization
Summary repeats previously mapped learning, policy and Q-learning concepts

gaps.finding: The source explicitly lists make, reset, step and render. Existing questions cover the first three but never distinguish rendering from stepping or from plotting a reward history. Add one coherent API lifecycle/observation trace, not separate trivial import questions.

The proposed extension to 20000+ episodes has no meaningful question. Combine the additional step budget, the nonzero exploration floor and expected non-greedy decisions with the fact that more samples do not by themselves establish convergence. State the continuing 50-step task and unique-greedy-action assumptions.

Current items cover one interior encoding, zero and qualitative resizing but not the actual physical intervals/saturation or a coherent 12-bin range-preserving encoder. Add an ideal-arithmetic boundary/range calculation with offset, width and clipping bounds stated; avoid floating boundary ambiguity.

Current questions identify off-policy labels and a maximum symbol but do not trace the distinction between the actually sampled reward, an estimated greedy bootstrap and an exploratory next action. Add a short nonzero-Q transition comparing these targets. Do not call the complete bootstrapped target an observed return.

scope: All 34 pages actually inspected; 28 original substantive pages plus one repeated summary have at least one citation. The author-style count of 74 one-question concept records is not a count of 74 independent unique source concepts. Four meaningful examination angles remain open; the pool also needs genuinely difficult synthesis and varied selection/statement formats rather than inflated medium labels. No complete-course claim.
